Under a quota trade deal between the US and Russia[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-114) the tribe were allowed to take 20 whales over the course of five years for 'cultural whaling'.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-115) The hunts had not occurred in 70 years due to the diminishment of the whale population by commercial whaling. In an attempt to scare the whales from the area, the group originally intended to use underwater speakers blasting the sounds of [killer whales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Killer_whale "Killer whale")[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-CBS_Worldwide_Corp_1998-10-01-116) as well as a small submarine painted to look like a killer whale.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-The_Seattle_Times_2005-10-08-117)

On November 2, Makah Tribal Police arrested four protesters who entered the reservation during the demonstration. All four were later released. Angry Makah seized an inflatable boat belonging to the group and threw rocks at the Sea Shepherd's 95-foot former Coast Guard vessel _Sirenian_.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-The_New_York_Times_1998-11-2-118) Sea Shepherd had two ships involved in a standoff that lasted 57 days before agreeing to withdraw on November 26.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-The_New_York_Times_1998-11-02-119)

Sea Shepherd returned to Neah Bay in 1999. They gathered locals and formed a blockade to prevent the whalers from leaving. However, the U.S. Coast Guard arrested Paul Watson's wife when she trespassed on the reservation, and eventually the Makah managed to kill one whale in May 1999. The event was well covered, and, due to public pressure garnered by Sea Shepherd's campaign, the Makah never resumed commercial whaling.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-ReferenceA-8)

**St. Lucia, St. Vincent and the Grenadines whaling (2001, 2003)**

In 2001, corresponding with the meeting of the IWC in St. Lucia, Sea Shepherd proved that St. Lucia killed whales on the same day the government denied it by photographing a slain juvenile pilot whale. Despite death threats, Sea Shepherd released the images. As a result, about 400 vacation bookings to St. Lucia were cancelled. Sea Shepherd later led an email campaign against the country's whaling.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-ReferenceA-8)

In 2003, Sea Shepherd posted a reward for information leading to the arrest of the person or people who murdered St. Lucian whale and dolphin conservationist Jane Tipson.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-ReferenceA-8)

### Japanese whaling (2003–2017)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Japanese whaling (2003–2017)")]

In its anti-whaling efforts, Sea Shepherd attempts to deter [Japanese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whaling_in_Japan "Whaling in Japan") ships that hunt [minke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minke_whale "Minke whale") and [fin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fin_whale "Fin whale") whales in the [Southern Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Ocean "Southern Ocean"). In 2005, Japan decided to double its quota from the previous year to 935 minke whales and ten [endangered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endangered "Endangered")[fin whales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fin_whales "Fin whales"). In 2007, they planned a take of 50 fin whales and 50 [humpback whales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humpback_whales "Humpback whales"). Sea Shepherd claims that its activities reduced catches to a level where the Japanese had not been able to make a profit from the whaling for three years running as of 2010.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-NEVER-120)

As of 2005, the Japanese fleet of the [Institute of Cetacean Research](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institute_of_Cetacean_Research "Institute of Cetacean Research") typically consists of a [factory ship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Factory_ship "Factory ship"), two spotter vessels, and three harpoon boats, though the exact fleet composition has varied. The whalers say that lethal research is needed to accurately measure the whale population, health, and response to global warming and is essential for the sustainable management of the world's cetacean stocks.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-National_Geographic-1) Australia and New Zealand have started a non-lethal whale research program to show that the Japanese lethal research program is no longer necessary.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-Telegraph_2008-11-17-121)[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-122) Sea Shepherd and other environmental groups dispute the Japanese statement of research "as a disguise for commercial whaling, which is banned."[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-Australia_condemns_Japanese_whalers-2)[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-Japanese_firms_end_whale_meat_sales-123)

Article III.2 of the ICRW,[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-INTERNATIONAL_CONVENTION_FOR_THE_REGULATION_OF_WHALING-124) however, requires that no [meat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whale_meat "Whale meat") from caught whales is wasted, and in order to meet this requirement as well as fund their efforts, the whalers sell the meat on the open market. Among other places, it can be found at Tokyo's famed [Tsukiji fish market](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsukiji_fish_market "Tsukiji fish market") and Japanese restaurants.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-National_Geographic-1) Sea Shepherd has stated that one of the main aims of their operations is to make commercial whaling financially unviable.

In his 2009 book, _Whaling in Japan_, Jun Morikawa states that Sea Shepherd's confrontational tactics have actually strengthened Japan's resolve to continue with its whaling program. According to Morikawa, Sea Shepherd's activities against Japan's whaling ships have allowed the Japanese government to rally domestic support for the program from Japanese who were otherwise ambivalent about the practice of hunting and eating whales.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-125)

August 2017, Sea Shepherd announced that they would suspend their anti-whaling activism. They cited the fleets inability to compete against the evolution of the whaling fleet supported with high tech military resources such as 'real time satellite' surveillance and increased funding. However Paul Watson claimed the organization will devise alternative undisclosed strategies to adapt in the future. He has criticized the Australian government for not providing logistical support to the organization such as satellite surveillance.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-126)

#### Japanese dolphin hunts (1982, 2003, 2010–present)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Japanese dolphin hunts (1982, 2003, 2010–present)")]

In 1982, Sea Shepherd negotiated an end to the dolphin slaughter in Iki Island, Japan. The agreement was broken twice by the Japanese fishermen, in 1993 and 1996, but has otherwise been respected.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-ReferenceB-127)

In October 2003, Sea Shepherd documented the method used to kill dolphins in the Japanese historic whaling town of [Taiji](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiji,_Wakayama "Taiji, Wakayama"). They say that Japanese fishermen use unnecessarily brutal [methods to hunt dolphins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiji_dolphin_drive_hunt "Taiji dolphin drive hunt").[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-128) In November, two members, including Watson's wife, were arrested for trying to free whales penned in a bay. It was also unclear exactly what species was involved. Watson stated they were dolphins, and Japanese officials said they were probably [pilot whales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pilot_whales "Pilot whales"), which are dolphins, as much as killer whales are dolphins.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-129) In 2004, The Cetacean Society International claimed that the Sea Shepherd's release of captured dolphins "played into the hands of the authorities" and prevented other groups from documenting the activities at Taiji.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-130)

In 2009, [Ian Campbell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Campbell_(Australian_politician) "Ian Campbell (Australian politician)"), a Sea Shepherd board member, called for a boycott of [Japan's 2016 Olympic bid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan's_2016_Olympic_bid "Japan's 2016 Olympic bid") because of the reported 23,000 dolphins killed each year at Taiji.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-131) Later that year, Sea Shepherd was featured in the documentary film The Cove, which brought the dolphin hunt in Taiji to international news.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-ReferenceB-127)

In 2010, Sea Shepherd returned to Taiji to document the slaughter, beginning Operation Infinite Patience. The first year saw the quota cut in half, and Sea Shepherd has returned to Taiji every year since. In 2015, Operation Infinite Patience turned into Operation Henkaku, with a stronger focus on the captive dolphin industry.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-132)

#### Southern Ocean (2005–2006)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Southern Ocean (2005–2006)")]

Between December 2005 and January 2006, a crew of 43 aboard the _Farley Mowat_ attempted to stop the Japanese whaling fleet in the [Southern Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Ocean "Southern Ocean"). During the campaign, the _Farley Mowat_ 'sideswiped' a Japanese supply ship called the _[Oriental Bluebird](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oriental\_Bluebird "Oriental Bluebird")_. No damage or injuries were reported.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-NZ_Herald_10363013-133) New Zealand Conservation Minister Chris Carter criticized Sea Shepherd as irresponsible for using tactics such as running into the other vessel with a "can opener" device, a seven-foot steel blade on the starboard bow designed to damage the hull of an enemy ship.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-National_Geographic-1)

Ian Campbell, Australia's environment minister, said Watson's threats to attack the Japanese fleet reflected poorly on legitimate anti-whaling groups and risked "setting back the cause of whale conservation many years." After Watson called the New Zealand government "contemptible"[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-134) for allowing Japan to continue killing whales, Campbell called Watson a "lunatic" and "rogue pirate on the seas." Watson dispatched a press release that he would stop his attacks if the governments of New Zealand and Australia would initiate legal action to stop the whaling.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-National_Geographic-1)

On January 16, the organization declared that its fuel supplies had run out and that they were heading to shore. They claimed credit for chasing the whalers from whaling grounds and hindering operations for over 15 days. The vessel covered more than 4000 km over a six-week period. The Japanese fell 83 whales short of their quota.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-135)

#### Operation Leviathan (2006–2007)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Operation Leviathan (2006–2007)")]

Between December 2006 and February 2007, the _Robert Hunter_ and _Farley Mowat_ participated in "Operation Leviathan" against Japanese whaling in the Southern Ocean. On February 9, 2007, Sea Shepherd was able to intercept the _Nisshin Maru_ and engaged it, but later had to stop and search for one of their missing small boats. On February 12, 2007, the group stated it had spotted the Japanese vessel _Kaiko Maru_ as it pursued a pod of minke whales and moved its vessels to intercept the hunt. The Institute for Cetacean Research in Tokyo said the _Robert Hunter_ rammed the _Kaiko Maru_ and that afterwards, both Sea Shepherd ships came to either side of the Kaiko Maru, stopping her from continuing. The Japanese stated that they then threw smoke pots on to the deck and released ropes and nets. The Japanese had already put out several distress calls due to a propeller they say was damaged during the attacks. Watson told the press that the _Farley Mowat_ chased the whaler into the ice and that the _Kaiko Maru_ then sideswiped the _Robert Hunter_ to push the ship into the ice. He also said that shortly after that, the _Kaiko Maru_ reversed and collided deliberately into the port stern section of the _Robert Hunter_ causing a metre-long gash in the starboard bow region.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-136) This campaign was featured in the documentary _[At the Edge of the World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/At\_the\_Edge\_of\_the\_World\_(2008\_film) "At the Edge of the World (2008 film)")_.

#### Operation Migaloo (2007–2008)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Operation Migaloo (2007–2008)")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/04/MV_Steve_Irwin_Melbourne.jpg/250px-MV_Steve_Irwin_Melbourne.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:MV_Steve_Irwin_Melbourne.jpg)

[MV _Steve Irwin_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MY_Steve_Irwin "MY Steve Irwin") arriving in Melbourne, 2008.

The 2007–08 Antarctic campaign was named Operation [Migaloo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Migaloo "Migaloo"), after the only known albino humpback in the world. This campaign was the focus of the first season of [Animal Planet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_Planet "Animal Planet")'s [reality TV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reality_television "Reality television") series _[Whale Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whale\_Wars "Whale Wars")_, which premiered on November 7, 2008.

On January 15, 2008, after attempting to entangle the whaling vessel's propeller and throwing containers of [butyric acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Butyric_acid "Butyric acid") onto the decks,[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-asahi-137) two Sea Shepherd members, Benjamin Potts and Giles Lane, from the Sea Shepherd vessel [MV _Steve Irwin_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MY_Steve_Irwin "MY Steve Irwin") boarded the Japanese whaling vessel _[Yushin Maru No. 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yushin\_Maru\_No.\_2 "Yushin Maru No. 2")_ from a rigid-hulled inflatable boat. The pair were delivering a letter advising the Japanese that they were "whaling illegally"[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-canada.com-138) with the hope of creating an international incident.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-Animal_Planet_2008-139) The Japanese responded by saying that the men would be held until Sea Shepherd stopped what they called "dangerous and illegal activities."[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-Stuff.co.nz_217328-140)

The crew of the _Yushin Maru No. 2_ detained the men for two days, before turning them over to the Australian customs vessel [MV _Oceanic Viking_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MV_Oceanic_Viking "MV Oceanic Viking") on the orders of Japanese authorities;[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-canada.com-138) subsequently, the _Steve Irwin_ rendezvoused with the _Oceanic Viking_ and the two crewmembers were returned to Sea Shepherd.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-asahi-137)[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-141)[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-142) On April 9, first mate Peter Brown was described in a newspaper article as saying that the incident only became a hostage situation because the Sea Shepherd vessel left the scene, so the Japanese would be forced to hold the two crewmen longer. He was quoted as saying, "It's all giant street theater."[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-cape_cod_times_2008-04-09-143)

On March 3, Sea Shepherd members threw bottles of butyric acid and packages of slippery [methyl cellulose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methyl_cellulose "Methyl cellulose") powder onto the Japanese vessel _[Nisshin Maru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nisshin\_Maru "Nisshin Maru")_. Australian foreign minister [Stephen Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Smith_(Australian_politician) "Stephen Smith (Australian politician)") condemned Sea Shepherd's actions for potentially causing injury[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-144) The Japanese Government called in the Australian and Netherlands ambassadors to protest the actions and urge those countries to prevent any violence.[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-145) Watson said: "They are so full of crap. We filmed and photographed the entire thing. Not a single thing landed anywhere near their crew ... It is their way of trying to get sympathy."[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-Darby-146)

The International Whaling Commission issued a statement on March 8, 2008, that "called upon the Sea Shepherd Conservation Society to refrain from dangerous actions that jeopardise safety at sea, and on vessels and crews concerned to exercise restraint."[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-147) The statement also reiterated earlier IWC resolutions from May and July 2007 that read in part, "The commission and its contracting governments do not condone and in fact condemn any actions that are a risk to human life and property in relation to the activities of vessels at sea."[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-148)[[149]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-149) The Australian Government also called for all parties to "exercise restraint" and "responsible behaviour" in the Southern Ocean.[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-150)

On March 17, 2008, Paul Watson claimed that he was shot by the Japanese crew or coast guard personnel during the campaign. The incident is heavily documented during the show in the final episode, and the first six episodes are covered as a buildup to what is portrayed as the major incident during the campaign. The footage in "Whale Wars" shows Watson standing on the deck of the _Steve Irwin_ while Sea Shepherd crew throws glass bottles filled with [butyric acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Butyric_acid "Butyric acid") at the _Nisshin Maru_ whaling vessel. The Japanese respond by throwing [flashbang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stun_grenade "Stun grenade") devices. Watson is then shown reaching inside his jacket and bullet-proof vest and remarking "I've been hit." Back inside the bridge of the _Steve Irwin_, a metal fragment is found inside the vest.[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-BBC_2008-03-07-151) The Institute of Cetacean Research has dismissed Sea Shepherd's statements as lies. The Institute and Coast Guard said that they used seven [flashbang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stun_grenade "Stun grenade") devices designed to flash and make noise in the air without causing harm.[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-152) Neither of the two conflicting accounts have been independently verified. The Australian Foreign Affairs Department had condemned "actions by crew members of any vessel that cause injury." Two media releases were made on the same day from the office. One said that the Australian Embassy in Tokyo had been informed by the Japanese that the whalers had "fired warning shots"[[153]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-153) while the updated version used the phrase "'warning balls'– also known as 'flashbangs'– had been fired", and that no gunshots had occurred.[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-154)

The [Tokyo Metropolitan Police Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo_Metropolitan_Police_Department "Tokyo Metropolitan Police Department") obtained arrest warrants for three Sea Shepherd crew (Daniel Bebawi, Jon Batchelor and Ralph Koo), for allegedly attempting to foul the propeller of the _Keiko Maru_ and throwing smoke bombs. Japanese authorities also requested to have the men placed on the [Interpol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interpol "Interpol") '[red notice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_notice "Red notice")' list.[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-155)

#### Operation Sparrow and Sparrow II

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Operation Sparrow and Sparrow II")]

[fr:Sea Shepherd Conservation Society#Opérations Sparrow et Sparrow II](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea%20Shepherd%20Conservation%20Society#Op%C3%A9rations_Sparrow_et_Sparrow_II "fr:Sea Shepherd Conservation Society")

These operations were intended to continue Thunder, a poaching vessel fishing for Patagonian toothfish in the Southern Ocean. It was chased for 110 days by the organization and was scuttled by his captain in the Gulf of Guinea in April 2015. In October 2015, the São Tomé and Príncipe justice system imposed penalties on a Chilean captain and two Spanish mechanics up to three years in prison and several million euros fine for "use of false fishing permits", "pollution of the sea" and "dangerous driving". In August 2017, the Spanish Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries sentenced to fines totaling more than 5.2 million euros, six citizens and six Spanish companies involved in this case.

Subsequently, in 2015, Sea Shepherd joined forces with the Gabonese government to create an intervention force controlling fishing boats during the season, which became operational the following year.

#### Operation Musashi (2008–2009)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Operation Musashi (2008–2009)")]

The 2008–2009 Antarctic campaign was named Operation Musashi after the 17th-century Japanese strategist [Miyamoto Musashi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miyamoto_Musashi "Miyamoto Musashi").[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-156) On December 4, 2008, actress [Daryl Hannah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daryl_Hannah "Daryl Hannah") joined Sea Shepherd's crew aboard the _Steve Irwin_ to take part in this season's operation.[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-157)

On February 6, 2009, Watson reported that the _Steve Irwin_ had collided with the _Yushin Maru 2_ as the _Steve Irwin_ tried to block its attempt to prevent the transfer of a dead whale up the slipway of the factory ship _Nisshin Maru_. As Watson explained the incident, "We were in the process of blocking the transfer from the _Yushin Maru 2_ when the _Yushin Maru 1_ moved directly in front of the bow to block us. I could not turn to starboard without hitting the _Yushin Maru 1_. I tried to back down but the movement of the _Yushin Maru 2_ made the collision unavoidable."[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-158) The Japanese whalers blamed Sea Shepherd for the crash, characterizing the incident as a "deliberate ramming."[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-159)[[160]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-160) The collision was filmed by cameramen for the _[Whale Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whale\_Wars "Whale Wars")_ reality series,[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-161) and formed part of a multi-day conflict during which Sea Shepherd attempted to prevent the Japanese fleet from harpooning whales, respectively tried to block whales from being transferred to the factory ship for processing by blockading the Japanese' vessel's [slipway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slipway "Slipway"). The Japanese made extensive use of [LRADs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Range_Acoustic_Device "Long Range Acoustic Device") to deter Sea Shepherd. They were also accused of aiming the device at the _Steve Irwin's_ helicopter while in flight, something the group especially condemned, seeing that the helicopter was only engaged in filming, and could have crashed if the pilot had lost control.[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-162)

Also in February, the president of the company overseeing the whale hunt used a media release to call upon the government of Australia to prevent what he considered violations of the [United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Convention_on_the_Law_of_the_Sea "United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea"). He expressed concerns over what he called "deliberately ramming vessels and trying to disable their propellers."[[163]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-163) When the _Steve Irwin_ returned to [Hobart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hobart "Hobart"), Australian Federal Police seized film footage and the ships logs.[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-Perth_Now-164)

#### Operation Waltzing Matilda (2009–2010)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Operation Waltzing Matilda (2009–2010)")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/56/Ady_Gil_2.jpg/250px-Ady_Gil_2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ady_Gil_2.jpg)

The _[Ady Gil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MY\_Ady\_Gil "MY Ady Gil")_ docked for repairs in [Hobart, Tasmania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hobart,_Tasmania "Hobart, Tasmania").

In June 2009, Sea Shepherd announced its 2009–10 Antarctic campaign, called Operation [Waltzing Matilda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waltzing_Matilda "Waltzing Matilda").[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-165) The campaign would include the record-breaking _[Earthrace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earthrace "Earthrace")_ vessel, now renamed _Ady Gil_ in honor of the benefactor who helped acquire the vessel for Sea Shepherd.[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-166) The _Ady Gil_ was a futuristic styled ship that held the world record for circumnavigation of the globe by a motorized vessel. The eco-friendly vessel usually ran on a low emission fuel "derived mainly from animal fat, soybeans or other forms of [bio-diesel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biodiesel "Biodiesel")"[[167]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-167) but was forced by operational reasons to switch to a more polluting petroleum diesel.[[168]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-168)[Pete Bethune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_James_Bethune "Peter James Bethune"), the operator, said that an agreement was reached with Sea Shepherd for the boat to adopt a support role.[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-The_Age_2009-06-29-169)[[170]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-wail_for_whales-170) Watson indicated that the _Ady Gil_ would be used to intercept and block harpoons.[[171]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-smh20090625-171) It was also reported that the MV _Steve Irwin_ was equipped with a new water cannon for this operation.[[172]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-most_dangerous_yet-172)

On January 5, 2010, Sea Shepherd announced that TV personality [Bob Barker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Barker "Bob Barker") had earlier donated $5 million to Sea Shepherd to buy in secret an ex-Norwegian whaling vessel, now named _[Bob Barker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MY\_Bob\_Barker "MY Bob Barker")_ after the donor, and that the ship located the _[Nisshin Maru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nisshin\_Maru "Nisshin Maru")_ Japanese whaling vessel. The _Bob Barker_ reportedly flew the Norwegian flag when within range of the Nisshin Maru. The Norwegian flag was then lowered and the '[Jolly Roger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jolly_Roger "Jolly Roger")' Sea Shepherd flag raised.[[173]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-bob_barker_ship-173) The _Bob Barker'_ s search for the whaling fleet was aided by a tip sent in from the [MV _Orion_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MV_Orion "MV Orion"), which happened upon the whaling fleet while on a cruise to Antarctica.[[174]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-Orion_finds_fleet-174)

In December 2009 and early 2010, New Zealand representatives of the [Institute of Cetacean Research](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institute_of_Cetacean_Research "Institute of Cetacean Research"), including PR specialist [Glenn Inwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenn_Inwood "Glenn Inwood"), chartered Australian planes to search for the other Sea Shepherd ship, MV _Steve Irwin_. Sea Shepherd claims that while doing so, they fraudulently posed as New Zealand government agents—but in any case failed to find the vessel.[[175]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-175)[[176]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-GURU-176) The plane hire by the Institute sparked protest from conservation groups and rival political parties of the Australian Government. While the Australian Government itself criticised the hire after it became known, the incident was still seen as failure of the current Labor government of Prime Minister Rudd to follow up on their election promises to strongly oppose Japanese whaling.[[177]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-NZ_Herald_10618800-177)[[178]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-SLAMS-178) The incident led to the introduction by [Rachel Siewert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Siewert "Rachel Siewert") of a Parliament bill to ban Japanese whalers from using Australian planes to spy on protesters.[[179]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-RUDDURGED-179)[[180]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-Greens_call_for_end_to_Aussie_spy_planes_aiding_Japanese_whaling-180)

Sea Shepherd reported that in this last season, the group had increasingly received information from private persons about the whereabouts of the Japanese fleet, such as by ship passengers on an Antarctic cruise who noted the fleet refueling.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-HARDLINE-3)

Japan's Fisheries Agency announced on April 12, 2010, that the whaling fleet had caught about half of the 985 whales it has hoped to catch during the 2009–2010 whaling research season as a result of obstruction by Sea Shepherd operations. The whalers harvested 506 southern minke whales and one finback whale.[[181]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-181)

##### Ady Gil collision (2010)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: Ady Gil collision (2010)")]

For the details of the incident, see _[MY Ady Gil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MY\_Ady\_Gil#Collision\_with\_the\_Sh%C5%8Dnan\_Maru\_2\_and\_abandonment "MY Ady Gil")_

On January 6, 2010, the _Ady Gil_ was severely damaged in the Antarctic Ocean after the Japanese security vessel the _[Shōnan Maru 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sh%C5%8Dnan\_Maru\_2 "Shōnan Maru 2")_ collided with it; both sides blamed each other for the incident.[[182]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-182) One of the six crewmen was injured.[[183]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-ady_gil_hit-183) Sea Shepherd attempted to tow the stricken vessel to an Antarctic research base where it could have been lifted aboard a larger ship, but the boat took on too much water and became too heavy on the tow.[[184]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-RESTRAINT-184) The _Ady Gil_ was abandoned on January 7, 2010, at 17:20 GMT.[[185]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-SUNK-185)

The [Australian Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Australia "Government of Australia"),[[183]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-ady_gil_hit-183) and the [New Zealand Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governments_of_New_Zealand "Governments of New Zealand") called for restraint and expressed concern at the risk of human lives in the hostile environment. The New Zealand government also repeated its opposition to whaling in the sanctuary.[[184]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-RESTRAINT-184) However, New Zealand's Foreign Minister [Murray McCully](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murray_McCully "Murray McCully") later stated that:

_"If people_ [referring to Sea Shepherd] _are determined to break the law and determined to kill other people on the high seas, then it is not the responsibility of the New Zealand Government or any other Government to send armed vessels down there or something of that sort to stop them."_[[186]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-RISK-186)
This brought a heated response by [Paul Watson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Watson "Paul Watson"), who accused the "know-nothing politician" McCully of ignoring the fact that Sea Shepherd had not killed anyone in over three decades of [direct action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_action "Direct action")—and stated that McCully's comments were instead giving Japanese whalers a green light to endanger the lives of Sea Shepherd crews.[[186]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-RISK-186)[[187]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-187)

A New Zealand spokesman for the Institute of Cetacean Research noted that Japan would continue to protect their operations "in whatever way it can" and that further clashes would be likely unless Sea Shepherd stopped its operations.[[184]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-RESTRAINT-184)

On January 9, 2010, Sea Shepherd lodged a piracy complaint against the captain and the crew of the _Shōnan Maru 2_ in the Dutch courts.[[188]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-188) It has also asked Australia and New Zealand to investigate charges against the Japanese, including for [attempted murder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attempted_murder "Attempted murder"),[[189]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-189) and proclaimed that had the situation been reversed, the Australian Navy would now be sending a ship to arrest him.[[190]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-STREET_FIGHT-190) After requests from the Australian Government, the [Government of Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Japan "Government of Japan") has stated that it would undertake "appropriate inquiries" into how the collision occurred, but accused Sea Shepherd of intentionally endangering the lives of crew.[[191]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-191) However, they also protested against the call for restraint on both sides, as they consider Sea Shepherd to blame for the "unlawful rampage."[[192]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-ATTACKS-192)

Sea Shepherd noted that after the loss of the vessel, a flood of donations had arrived for the group, with $170,000 being given in the first few hours after the collision.[[193]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-193)

On February 15, 2010, it was reported that [Pete Bethune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_James_Bethune "Peter James Bethune"), the former captain of the _Ady Gil_, boarded the _Shonan Maru_ at night for the purpose of making a [citizen's arrest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citizen's_arrest "Citizen's arrest") of its captain for attempted murder of his own crew and the destruction of the _Ady Gil_. Bethune, who reportedly had to overcome spikes and anti-boarding nets to board the Japanese vessel, was also to present the captain with a bill for US$3 million and a letter outlining the findings of maritime experts who found that the Japanese vessel was at fault for the collision as it was the overtaking vessel and did not have right of way.[[194]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-ARREST-194)[[195]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-BOARDED-195) According to the crew of the Shonan Maru, Bethune had thrown butyric acid onto the ship, giving a chemical burn to one sailor. Paul Watson, group founder and captain of the _Steve Irwin_, said that the mission was intended as a message to the [New Zealand government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_New_Zealand "Government of New Zealand") which the SSCS accuses of hypocrisy and failure to represent the interests of the _Ady Gil_ and its captain. In an interview, Watson said, "If we had sunk a Japanese vessel we would now be under arrest by the Australian navy."[[194]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-ARREST-194) Meanwhile, New Zealand's government was being criticised by the main opposition party of "washing their hands" of Mr. Bethune's fate (despite the government offering consular assistance), after Foreign Minister McCully declared that Bethune must have been well aware of the consequences of his actions.[[196]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-ANGER-196)

Japan's foreign minister, [Katsuya Okada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katsuya_Okada "Katsuya Okada"), announced that Bethune was being detained under international maritime law and would be transported to Japan, where he would face charges, possibly of piracy.[[197]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations#cite_note-DETA

# Sea Shepherd vs. IUU Fishing: A Decade of Action and Impact

By[devon11](https://seashepherd.org/author/devonfa97bdcbb9/)December 10, 2024 September 27th, 2026[No Comments](https://seashepherd.org/2024/12/10/iuu-fishing-sea-shepherds-fight-a-decade-of-action-and-impact/#respond)

Illegal Fishing

Sea Shepherd vs. IUU Fishing

Illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing poses an incredible threat to marine ecosystems and the livelihoods of coastal communities worldwide. Since 2016, Sea Shepherd has actively partnered with African coastal nations to combat this pervasive issue.

Sea Shepherd’s Partnerships and Operations

Sea Shepherd collaborates with national authorities to enhance surveillance and enforcement in African waters. Sea Shepherd has provided civilian offshore patrol vessels, operational crews, and fuel, empowering local enforcement agencies to uphold fisheries laws. These initiatives include:

*   **Operation Albacore**: Launched in April 2016 in partnership with Gabon, this operation expanded to São Tomé and Príncipe, leading to the inspection of over 40 vessels and the arrest of five for illegal fishing activities.
*   **Operation Jodari**: Beginning in January 2018 with the Tanzanian government, this campaign resulted in multiple arrests for violating shark finning laws and labor abuse.

Protecting Africa’s Biodiversity

Africa’s coastal waters are rich in biodiversity, hosting numerous fish species, sharks, whales, and dolphins. Many of these areas lack the resources to monitor and protect marine environments, making them vulnerable to IUU fishing. This illegal activity not only depletes fish stocks but also threatens the entire marine ecosystem.

Sea Shepherd's Fight Continues

Sea Shepherd is dedicated to expanding its efforts by forging new government partnerships, aiming to cover and protect more of these incredibly critical coastlines across the globe.

We know that through collaborative efforts with governments and local authorities we can protect, conserve and defend these vital ocean ecosystems that the world’s health depends on.

To learn more about our efforts in Africa visit: [DefenceWeb](https://www.defenceweb.co.za/security/maritime-security/sea-shepherd-helps-fight-fisheries-crime-in-namibia/)

The **Sea Shepherd Conservation Society** (**SSCS**) is a [non-profit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-profit "Non-profit"), [marine conservation activism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_conservation_activism "Marine conservation activism") organization based in [Friday Harbor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friday_Harbor,_Washington "Friday Harbor, Washington") on [San Juan Island, Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Juan_Island,_Washington "San Juan Island, Washington"), in the United States.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-1) Sea Shepherd employs [direct action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_action "Direct action") tactics to achieve its goals,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-2) most famously by deploying its fleet of ships to track, report on and actively impede the work of [fishing vessels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fishing_vessel "Fishing vessel") they believe to be engaged in illegal and unregulated activities causing the unsustainable exploitation of marine life.

Sea Shepherd has been criticised by some environmental groups and national governments that oppose its tactics.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-Greenpeace-3) The Japanese government, whose [whaling industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whaling_in_Japan "Whaling in Japan") is a leading target of the organization's efforts, has called Sea Shepherd [eco-terrorists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eco-terrorism "Eco-terrorism") for "impeding their research".[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-Telegraph_2009-04-17-4)

## History

Main article: [Sea Shepherd Conservation Society operations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations "Sea Shepherd Conservation Society operations")

The predecessor organization of Sea Shepherd, the "Earth Force Society", was formed in 1977, after its founder, [Paul Watson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Watson "Paul Watson"), was ousted from the board of [Greenpeace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenpeace "Greenpeace") for disagreements over his [direct action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_action "Direct action") activism which clashed with their [pacifist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacifism "Pacifism") nature.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-Guardian-5) Watson soon left Greenpeace. Initially without funding and with only a small group of supporters, Watson convinced [Cleveland Amory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland_Amory "Cleveland Amory"), head of the Fund for Animals, to fund Watson's first vessel, the _Sea Shepherd_ in 1978.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-The_New_Yorker_2007-11-05-6)

The first direct action undertaken by the organization was against Canadian [seal hunting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seal_hunting "Seal hunting") in the [Gulf of St. Lawrence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Saint_Lawrence "Gulf of Saint Lawrence") in March 1979.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-8) The same year, the Sea Shepherd also rammed an unregulated Portuguese whaling vessel,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-9) the notorious _Sierra_.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-Nagtzaam-10) After the [Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portugal "Portugal") campaign, the first _Sea Shepherd_ had to be [scuttled](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scuttling "Scuttling"), but Watson sold the story to raise money to fund his next vessel.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-The_New_Yorker_2007-11-05-6) He then spent the 1980s undertaking a variety of controversial and dangerous operations in support of various [marine conservation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_conservation "Marine conservation") aims,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-The_New_Yorker_2007-11-05-6) and physically intervened against Russian, Spanish, Norwegian, Icelandic, [Makah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Makah "Makah"), [Faroese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whaling_in_the_Faroe_Islands "Whaling in the Faroe Islands"), and Japanese whalers.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-The_New_Yorker_2007-11-05-6)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-National_Geographic-11)

In the 1990s the group is described as having undertaken a shift in its public attitude.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-The_New_Yorker_2007-11-05-6) Having previously argued primarily from an [ethical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethics "Ethics") viewpoint, Sea Shepherd began to describe itself as an [anti-poaching](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-poaching "Anti-poaching") agency, a claim it based on its interpretation of the [maritime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Admiralty_law "Admiralty law") and [conservation law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservation_law "Conservation law").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-The_New_Yorker_2007-11-05-6)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-Hollywood_Today_2009-06-09-12) The decade also saw the organization make more progress in saving wildlife, including by teaming up with other groups to reduce the prevalence of [driftnet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Driftnet "Driftnet") fishing. In 1994, Sea Shepherd sank an illegal Norwegian whaling vessel. However, no charges were brought as the vessel had been involved in even more illegal behavior than anticipated by the authorities.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-Our_History_2018-13)

The organization began in the 2000s by assisting with the clean up of the [Petrobras oil spill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_Northeast_Brazil_oil_spill "2019 Northeast Brazil oil spill"), [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil "Brazil")'s worst oil spill to date, after being contracted by the Rio government to mitigate against the devastation.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-Our_History_2018-13) Sea Shepherd also cooperated with other governments against maritime [poaching](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poaching "Poaching"), including in [Costa Rica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica "Costa Rica"), though not always with good outcomes.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-14) In 2008, Sea Shepherd conducted two trips around [Antarctica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antarctica "Antarctica") to disrupt illegal whaling practices.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-Our_History_2018-13)

Since 2014, Sea Shepherd has increasingly co-operated with national governments in assisting [anti-poaching](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-poaching "Anti-poaching") activity in national territorial waters and [marine reserves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_reserve "Marine reserve"), including with the [Italian Coast Guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_Coast_Guard "Italian Coast Guard") in [Sicily](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sicily "Sicily") (Operation Siracusa),[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-16)[Mexican Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexican_Navy "Mexican Navy") (Operation Milagro) and the Coastguards of [Gabon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabon "Gabon") and [São Tomé and Príncipe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A3o_Tom%C3%A9_and_Pr%C3%ADncipe "São Tomé and Príncipe") (Operation Albacore), which saw [Gabonese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabon "Gabon") military marines sail aboard Sea Shepherd vessels.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In late 2022, a schism occurred after Paul Watson was removed from the board of directors of Sea Shepherd Global, a move which, he says, was due to the organization shifting away from his policy of independent, direct action to one of collaboration with governments. Watson subsequently formed his own organization, the [Captain Paul Watson Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_Paul_Watson_Foundation?action=edit&redlink=1 "Captain Paul Watson Foundation (page does not exist)"), and a competing Sea Shepherd group called Sea Shepherd Origins. The France, UK, and Brazil chapters of Sea Shepherd have pledged their allegiance to Paul Watson and Sea Shepherd Origins, and have left the umbrella of Sea Shepherd Global. Neither Sea Shepherd Global or the regional chapters that remain loyal to it have issued statements in regard to these events.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-Schism_1-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-Schism_2-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-Schism_3-19)

## Organization

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/32/Farley_Mowat%2C_Melbourne.jpg/250px-Farley_Mowat%2C_Melbourne.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Farley_Mowat,_Melbourne.jpg)

A wildlife advocate during an education session on board [RV _Farley Mowat_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RV_Farley_Mowat "RV Farley Mowat")

Sea Shepherd is a non-governmental, non-profit environmental organization. In the United States it has a [501(c)(3)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/501_(c)#501(c)(3) "501 (c)") tax exempt status. Most of the organization's revenue is spent on its programs – 89.9 percent in 2019, with just 10.1 percent spent on administrative costs and [fundraising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundraising "Fundraising"). Sea Shepherd has also been rated highly for [financial transparency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transparency_(market) "Transparency (market)") and accountability.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-20) The group is supported by private and corporate donations, lectures by Watson, internet advertising and grants. It is operated by volunteers and a small paid staff, and is committed to staying small and with low spending on fundraising or recruitment.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-The_New_Yorker_2007-11-05-6)

Sea Shepherd is governed by a [board of directors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Board_of_directors "Board of directors") and several boards of advisers, each addressing an area of expertise. The Scientific, Technical and Conservation Advisory Board includes [Earth First!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth_First! "Earth First!") founder [Dave Foreman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Foreman "Dave Foreman") and Horst Klienschmidt, a former deputy chair of the [International Whaling Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Whaling_Commission "International Whaling Commission") (2006). The Legal and Law Enforcement Advisory Board includes [Ian Campbell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Campbell_(Australian_politician) "Ian Campbell (Australian politician)"), a former Australian Minister of the Environment and Heritage (2004–07).[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-22) The Animal Welfare, Humane and Animal Rights Advisory Board included [animal rights philosopher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_rights "Animal rights")[Tom Regan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Regan "Tom Regan"), until his death in 2017. There is also a Media and Arts Advisory Board, Photography Advisory Board and a Financial and Management Advisory Board.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Direct action activism

Main article: [Sea Shepherd Conservation Society operations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society_operations "Sea Shepherd Conservation Society operations")

Sea Shepherd engages in conventional [protests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protest "Protest") and [direct actions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_action "Direct action") to protect marine wildlife. Sea Shepherd operations have included interdiction against [commercial fishing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commercial_fishing "Commercial fishing"), [shark poaching](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shark "Shark") and [finning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shark_finning "Shark finning"), [seal hunting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seal_hunting "Seal hunting"), and [whaling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whaling "Whaling").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-National_Geographic-11)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-Australia_condemns_Japanese_whalers-23) The group has been active in intervening against fishing and poaching in the [South Pacific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Ocean "Pacific Ocean"), the [Mediterranean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mediterranean_Sea "Mediterranean Sea"), and in waters around the [Galapagos Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galapagos_Islands "Galapagos Islands"). In addition to their direct action campaigns, Sea Shepherd works on ocean issues such as [plastic pollution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plastic_pollution "Plastic pollution"). Sea Shepherd chapters across the world organize [onshore cleanups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beach_cleaning "Beach cleaning") throughout the year to pick up debris near oceans, streams, and rivers. In April 2018, Sea Shepherd released a [PSA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_service_announcement "Public service announcement") that takes an artistic approach to telling target audiences that more than one million marine animals die every year from plastic debris.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-24)

According to its mission statement, Sea Shepherd "uses innovative direct-action tactics to investigate, document, and take action when necessary to expose and confront illegal activities on the high seas".[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-25) In addition to the organization's role of documenting and reporting violations of [conservation laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservation_law "Conservation law"), Sea Shepherd operations have utilized direct, non-lethal tactics including [scuttling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scuttling "Scuttling") and disabling whaling vessels at harbor,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-Telegraph_2009-04-17-4) intervening in Canadian and [Namibian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Namibia "Namibia")[seal hunts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seal_hunting "Seal hunting"),[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-26) shining [laser light](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dazzler_(weapon) "Dazzler (weapon)") at whalers,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-27) throwing bottles of foul-smelling [butyric acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Butyric_acid "Butyric acid") onto vessels at sea,[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-HARDLINE-28) boarding whaling vessels to protest while at sea, and seizing and destroying [drift nets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drift_net "Drift net") at sea. Sea Shepherd argues that these tactics are necessary to uncover and impede actions that violate international laws protecting wildlife, as the international community has shown itself unwilling or unable to stop species-endangering whaling and fishing practices.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-The_New_Yorker_2007-11-05-6)

Sea Shepherd staff and equipment have also been on the receiving end of physical violence by members of the fishing industry. In November 1998, [Makah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Makah_people "Makah people") seized an inflatable boat belonging to the group and threw rocks at the Sea Shepherd's _Sirenian_ in response to protests over their whale hunt.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-29) In 2005, 11 Sea Shepherd crew were involved in an altercation with sealers while on the ice. The sealers were not charged with any crime, but the activists were arrested and later convicted for approaching too close to the hunt.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-32) In 2008, fishermen in the French islands of [Saint Pierre and Miquelon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Pierre_and_Miquelon "Saint Pierre and Miquelon") cut the [mooring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mooring_(watercraft) "Mooring (watercraft)") lines of the _Farley Mowat_ after hearing Watson make disparaging comments about the deaths of four seal hunters.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-33)

In 2009, Paul Watson claimed the organization has sunk ten whaling ships while also destroying millions of dollars' worth of equipment.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-34) Their practice of attacking and sinking other ships has led to reports of injuries to other sailors as well as the Sea Shepherd crew, including concussions and complications from chemical attacks.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-acid-35)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-Darby-36) Watson considers the actions of Sea Shepherd to be against criminal operations and has called the group an anti-poaching organization.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-Hollywood_Today_2009-06-09-12) Critics claim that Sea Shepherd's actions constitute violations of international law,[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-37) while Watson has stated that Sea Shepherd believes that their actions constitute an attempt to enforce international conservation laws and international [maritime law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maritime_law "Maritime law") under the [World Charter for Nature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Charter_for_Nature "World Charter for Nature") adopted by the [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-39) Australia has declared Japan's hunt in the [Southern Ocean Whale Sanctuary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Ocean_Whale_Sanctuary "Southern Ocean Whale Sanctuary") to be illegal, and federal court judge Jim Allsop has stated "there is no practical mechanism by which orders of this court can be enforced".[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-new_scientist_2008-01-15-40) The lack of official enforcement mechanisms in the law prompted Sea Shepherd to adopt, without official sanction, what it sees as a law enforcement mission. A 2008 academic paper by researchers at [Monash University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monash_University "Monash University") in [Melbourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melbourne "Melbourne"), [Victoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_(Australia) "Victoria (Australia)"), concluded that Sea Shepherd's approach could constitute [vigilantism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vigilantism "Vigilantism"), because its seeks to enforce a legal status quo in the face of the international community's "inabilities or unwillingness to do so".[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-Nagtzaam-10)

### Anti-whaling controversy

See also: [International Convention for the Regulation of Whaling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Convention_for_the_Regulation_of_Whaling "International Convention for the Regulation of Whaling") and [Whaling in Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whaling_in_Japan "Whaling in Japan")

Watson left [Greenpeace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenpeace "Greenpeace") in 1977 after being voted off the [board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Board_of_directors "Board of directors") over his confrontational methods.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-41) Since then, Greenpeace has criticized Sea Shepherd for the group's tactics, particularly regarding its interaction with [whaling ships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whaler "Whaler") while at sea.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-42) The rival environmental group maintains Sea Shepherd is a violent organization whose tactics may endanger the lives of fishermen and whalers, and has labelled Watson an extremist.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-Telegraph_2009-04-17-4)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-43)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-44) Greenpeace has also stated: "By making it easy to paint [anti-whaling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-whaling "Anti-whaling") forces as dangerous, [piratical terrorists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piracy_in_the_21st_century "Piracy in the 21st century"), Sea Shepherd could undermine the forces within Japan which could actually bring whaling to an end".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-Greenpeace-3) In his 2009 book, _Whaling in Japan_, Jun Morikawa stated that Sea Shepherd's confrontational tactics had strengthened Japan's resolve to continue with its whaling program by helping to rally domestic support from Japanese citizens who might otherwise have been ambivalent about the practice of hunting and eating whales.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-45)

In March 2014 the [International Court of Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Court_of_Justice "International Court of Justice") ruled Japan's whaling program was not for scientific purposes. The Court ordered that Japan "revoke any extant authorization, permit or licence to kill, take or treat whales" and refrain from granting any further permits."[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-outcome_2014-46) In response to the court ruling, Japan cut its annual whaling quota from 915 to 333. The new quota included only [minke whales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minke_whale "Minke whale"), and ended the hunting of [humpback whales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humpback_whale "Humpback whale") and [fin whales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fin_whale "Fin whale").[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-47) Paul Watson said: "I think we've done an amazing job reducing their quotas and saving whales," and claimed the actions of Sea Shepherd were a major factor behind Japan's decision.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-48) In 2017, Sea Shepherd said it would stop sending ships to the Antarctic Ocean in pursuit of Japanese whalers, citing Japan's increased use of military surveillance satellites and passage of [anti-terrorism laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-terrorism_legislation "Anti-terrorism legislation") specifically to thwart Sea Shepherd.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-Pursuit2018-49)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-cnn.com-50) Japan passed new anti-terrorism legislation in view of the coming [2020 Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Summer_Olympics "2020 Summer Olympics"), but among its elements, the new law declared the presence of eco-activist vessels near whalers a terrorist offence. The combined measures were deemed to make Sea Shepherd's Antarctic operations no longer productive, with Watson noting his organisation "cannot compete with their military-grade technology".[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-Pursuit2018-49)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-51)

## Public relations

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f9/MV_Bob_Barker_in_port_2010-03-06.jpg/250px-MV_Bob_Barker_in_port_2010-03-06.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:MV_Bob_Barker_in_port_2010-03-06.jpg)

A $5 million donation from [Bob Barker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Barker "Bob Barker") facilitated the purchase of the [MY _Bob Barker_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MY_Bob_Barker "MY Bob Barker"), pictured here docked in [Hobart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hobart "Hobart"), [Tasmania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tasmania "Tasmania").

The Sea Shepherd Conservation Society has been called "media savvy" for their use of the press.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-National_Geographic-11)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-Montreal_Mirror_1997-06-05-52) The group has worked with journalists and has made statements through press releases to spread its message during various campaigns.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-Seattle_Times_1998-11-03-53)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-The_Age_2006-01-14-54)

Watson's public relations efforts are shown in an episode of _[Whale Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whale\_Wars "Whale Wars")_ when he creates an international "media storm"[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-Animal_Planet_103-55) after two Sea Shepherd crewmembers are detained on a Japanese whaling vessel. In his book, _Earthforce!_, Watson advises readers to make up facts and figures when they need to and to deliver them to reporters confidently.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-The_New_Yorker_2007-11-05-6) He also states that the "truth is irrelevant" due to the nature of mass media.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-56) In response to criticism that he manipulates the media, Watson has stated: "What we do is provide the media with the kind of stories they can't resist... and this is how we bring attention to what's happening to the whales, the seals, the sharks and the other marine conservation campaigns we're involved in."[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-Telegraph_2009-04-17-4)

Sea Shepherd has also used [satellite uplinks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communications_satellite "Communications satellite"), webcams, and internet blogging during its operations in the [Southern Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Ocean "Southern Ocean"), and has invited the media to ride along.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-57) In 2006, representatives from [Seven network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_network "Seven network") and _[National Geographic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National\_Geographic\_(magazine) "National Geographic (magazine)")_ magazine, along with documentary filmmakers, accompanied the group.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-National_Geographic-11) In a television series entitled _[Whale Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whale\_Wars "Whale Wars")_, [Discovery Communications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_Communications "Discovery Communications"), Inc. documented Sea Shepherd's 2008/09 Antarctic campaign against Japanese whalers, following events on the _Steve Irwin_.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-Telegraph_2009-04-17-4) The program premiered on November 7, 2008, on Discovery's [Animal Planet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_Planet "Animal Planet") network.

Aerial perspective of the Sea Shepherd docked at the Victoria Harbour Promenade, Waterfront end of Enterprize Way, [Docklands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Docklands,_Victoria "Docklands, Victoria"), February 2019

Sea Shepherd has received financial contributions from celebrities and businessmen such as entrepreneur [Steve Wynn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Wynn "Steve Wynn"), television personality [Bob Barker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Barker "Bob Barker"), and [John Paul DeJoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Paul_DeJoria "John Paul DeJoria"), as well as other celebrities.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-The_New_Yorker_2007-11-05-6)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-Hollywood_Today_2009-06-09-12)[Martin Sheen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Sheen "Martin Sheen"), [Daryl Hannah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daryl_Hannah "Daryl Hannah"), and [Richard Dean Anderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Dean_Anderson "Richard Dean Anderson") have joined the group during protests. Actors including [Edward Norton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Norton "Edward Norton"), [Pierce Brosnan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierce_Brosnan "Pierce Brosnan"), [Christian Bale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_Bale "Christian Bale"), [Clive Standen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clive_Standen "Clive Standen") and [Emily Deschanel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emily_Deschanel "Emily Deschanel") have supported the group through contributions,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-Telegraph_2009-04-17-4) while [William Shatner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Shatner "William Shatner") has also been mentioned as supporting the group.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-DOWNED-58) Actress and model [Pamela Anderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pamela_Anderson "Pamela Anderson") is an active spokesperson for the group, has participated in several campaigns, served on the board of directors and is a close friend of founder Paul Watson. In 2007, actor [Heath Ledger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heath_Ledger "Heath Ledger") conceived and directed a music video of the [Modest Mouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modest_Mouse "Modest Mouse") song "[King Rat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Rat_(song) "King Rat (song)")", intended to raise awareness of the whale hunts taking place each year off the coast of his native Australia. Although Ledger died before the video could be completed, others finished it in his honor and debuted the video online in August 2009. Proceeds from [iTunes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ITunes "ITunes") sales of the video in its first month of release were donated to Sea Shepherd.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-59)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Shepherd_Conservation_Society#cite_note-60)

From the music industry, [Anthony Kiedis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Kiedis "Anthony Kiedis") of the [Red Hot Chili Peppers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Hot_Chili_Peppers "Red Hot Chili Peppers"), [Leona Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leona_Lewis "Leona Lewis"), [Rick Rubin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Rubin "Rick Rubin"), and the groups ## Fleet of ships

For the main article on Sea Shepherd's fleet, see [Neptune's Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neptune's_Navy "Neptune's Navy").
